transcript.en: A university once left a storage bucket of student records open to the internet. No one hacked anything. A default setting was simply never changed. Today: the classic design principles for secure systems, how STRIDE finds threats before attackers do, and how to teach both without a list to memorise. Security aims at three properties. Confidentiality keeps data from the wrong people. Integrity keeps it from being changed without permission. Availability keeps it there when the right people need it. In nineteen seventy five, Saltzer and Schroeder listed design principles that still hold. Fail-safe defaults mean deny unless allowed. Least privilege means give only what is needed. Complete mediation means check every access. Industry breach reports repeatedly find that stolen credentials, phishing and misconfiguration start most incidents. Exotic exploits are a small share. That is a lesson for what we teach first. Threat modelling asks what could go wrong before it does. Draw the data flows, mark trust boundaries, and walk each element through STRIDE: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege. Principles taught as a list are forgotten by the exam. Instead, threat-model a system students use every day, like the university portal. Each team draws the data flow and finds one threat per STRIDE letter. Quick check! The open bucket was readable by anyone because access was allowed until someone blocked it. Which principle did it break? Fail-safe defaults. Access should be denied unless someone grants it on purpose. A secure system is safe before anyone configures it. In the app, open the breach lab. Set up the five accounts, let the forum get hacked, and name the principle each defence applies. Your turn. A student edits a hidden form field to change their grade before it is saved. Which STRIDE threat is that? Tampering. Remember: deny by default, give least privilege, check every access, and use STRIDE on a real system before attackers do. Try it in your next lecture: give teams a one-page data flow of the course registration system. Each team must find one threat for every STRIDE letter and propose a fix.

body.en:
Saltzer and Schroeder (1975) set out design principles for protecting information that remain the backbone of secure engineering: economy of mechanism, fail-safe defaults, complete mediation, open design, separation of privilege, least privilege, least common mechanism and psychological acceptability. Most real breaches are failures of these principles rather than of cryptography: default-open storage, over-privileged accounts, unchecked access paths. Anderson’s Security Engineering (2020) documents many such cases.

Threat modelling applies the principles systematically before deployment. Draw a data-flow diagram of processes, data stores, external entities and flows; mark trust boundaries where data crosses between privilege levels; then ask, for each element, how it could suffer spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service or elevation of privilege (STRIDE; Shostack, 2014). Each threat maps to a property (authentication, integrity, non-repudiation, confidentiality, availability, authorisation) and to a mitigation.

Principles taught as a list are rarely transferred. Threat-modelling a system students already use, such as the university portal or the course’s own submission system, makes the principles concrete and produces artefacts you can assess: a diagram, a threat table and a prioritised mitigation plan.
body.ar:
وضع Saltzer وSchroeder (١٩٧٥) مبادئ تصميم لحماية المعلومات ما زالت عماد الهندسة الآمنة: بساطة الآلية، والإعدادات الافتراضية الآمنة، والوساطة الكاملة، والتصميم المفتوح، وفصل الصلاحيات، وأقل صلاحية، وأقل آلية مشتركة، والقبول النفسي. ومعظم الاختراقات الحقيقية إخفاقات في هذه المبادئ لا في التشفير: تخزين مفتوح افتراضيًا، وحسابات بصلاحيات زائدة، ومسارات وصول غير مفحوصة. ويوثّق كتاب Anderson في هندسة الأمن (٢٠٢٠) حالات كثيرة من هذا النوع.

وتطبّق نمذجة التهديدات المبادئ بانتظام قبل النشر. ارسم مخطط مسار البيانات للعمليات ومخازن البيانات والكيانات الخارجية والتدفقات، وعلّم حدود الثقة حيث تعبر البيانات بين مستويات الصلاحية، ثم اسأل لكل عنصر كيف قد يتعرض للانتحال أو العبث أو الإنكار أو كشف المعلومات أو تعطيل الخدمة أو رفع الصلاحية (STRIDE، Shostack، ٢٠١٤). ويقابل كل تهديد خاصية (التحقق من الهوية، والسلامة، وعدم الإنكار، والسرية، والإتاحة، والتفويض) وإجراءً للحد منه.

ونادرًا ما تنتقل المبادئ التي تُدرَّس قائمةً. أما نمذجة تهديدات نظام يستخدمه الطلاب أصلًا، كبوابة الجامعة أو نظام تسليم المقرر نفسه، فتجعل المبادئ ملموسة وتنتج مخرجات يمكنك تقييمها: مخططًا وجدول تهديدات وخطة حد مرتّبة حسب الأولوية.

transcript.en: Every time a student opens the university portal, their browser agrees a secret key with a server it has never met, over a network anyone can listen to. How is that possible? Today: how two strangers agree a secret in public, how RSA encrypts and signs, and how to teach the number theory without losing the class. Public-key cryptography rests on functions that are easy one way and hard to reverse. Multiplying two large primes is easy. Factoring the product is believed to be hard. So is undoing modular exponentiation. Alice and Bob publicly agree a prime p and a base g. Each picks a secret and sends g to that power. Each then raises what they received to their own secret. Both reach the same key, and a listener cannot. With p twenty three and g five, Alice picks six and sends eight. Bob picks fifteen and sends nineteen. Both compute two as the shared key. RSA picks two primes and publishes their product n with an exponent e. Only the owner knows d, which undoes e. Anyone can encrypt with the public key. Signing reverses the roles: only the owner can sign, and anyone can verify. Start with the paint-mixing analogy: mixing colours is easy, unmixing is hard. Then let students run Diffie–Hellman by hand with tiny primes. The common misconception is that encryption alone proves who sent a message. It does not. Quick check! Bob encrypts a message with Alice's public key. Who can decrypt it? Only Alice, with her private key. Not even Bob can decrypt it afterwards. But Alice cannot tell it came from Bob, because anyone could have used her public key. In the app, open the public-key lab. Make a small RSA key pair, sign a message, change one letter and watch the check fail, then pick bigger primes and see the work of splitting n grow. Your turn. Plain Diffie–Hellman has no authentication. What can an attacker who controls the network do? Run a separate exchange with each side and relay everything. Remember: one-way functions make public keys possible, signatures prove origin, and key exchange needs authentication. Try it in your next lecture: put students in threes as Alice, Bob and Eve. They run Diffie–Hellman with p twenty three on paper, and Eve tries to find the key from what she hears.

body.en:
Diffie and Hellman (1976) showed that two parties can agree a shared secret over a public channel. With public prime p and generator g, Alice sends A = gᵃ mod p, Bob sends B = gᵇ mod p, and both compute gᵃᵇ mod p. An eavesdropper who sees A and B must compute gᵃᵇ mod p from them (the Diffie–Hellman problem); the best known way is to solve the discrete logarithm problem, believed infeasible for well-chosen large groups. Because the exchange authenticates no one, an active attacker can run separate exchanges with each side; real protocols such as TLS sign the exchange with certified keys.

RSA (Rivest, Shamir and Adleman, 1978) publishes n = pq and an exponent e; the private exponent d satisfies e × d ≡ 1 mod φ(n). Encryption computes c = mᵉ mod n and decryption m = cᵈ mod n. Signatures use the private key on a hash of the message, so anyone with the public key can verify origin and integrity. Textbook RSA is insecure; practical use requires padding such as OAEP for encryption and PSS for signatures (Katz and Lindell, Introduction to Modern Cryptography).

Common student misconceptions are that encryption alone authenticates the sender, that public keys are secret, and that larger keys fix protocol flaws. Paper simulations with tiny numbers, role-played man-in-the-middle attacks, and asking students to state exactly what each operation guarantees address these directly.
body.ar:
بيّن Diffie وHellman (١٩٧٦) أن طرفين يستطيعان الاتفاق على سر مشترك عبر قناة عامة. فمع عدد أولي عام p ومولّد g، ترسل أليس ⁦A = gᵃ mod p⁩، ويرسل بوب ⁦B = gᵇ mod p⁩، ويحسب كلاهما gᵃᵇ mod p. والمتصنّت الذي يرى A وB عليه أن يحسب منهما gᵃᵇ mod p (مسألة ديفي وهيلمان)، وأفضل طريقة معروفة لذلك حل مسألة اللوغاريتم المتقطع، ويُعتقد أنها غير ممكنة عمليًا لمجموعات كبيرة مختارة جيدًا. ولأن التبادل لا يتحقق من هوية أحد، يستطيع مهاجم نشط إجراء تبادلين منفصلين مع كل طرف، لذا توقّع البروتوكولات الحقيقية مثل TLS التبادلَ بمفاتيح موثّقة بشهادات.

وفي نظام RSA، الذي قدّمه Rivest وShamir وAdleman عام ١٩٧٨، يُنشر ⁦n = pq⁩ وأسٌّ e، ويحقق الأس الخاص d العلاقة ⁦e × d ≡ 1 mod φ(n)⁩. فالتشفير يحسب ⁦c = mᵉ mod n⁩، والفك ⁦m = cᵈ mod n⁩. وتستخدم التوقيعات المفتاح الخاص على تجزئة الرسالة، فيستطيع أي شخص لديه المفتاح العام التحقق من المصدر والسلامة. وRSA بصيغته المدرسية غير آمن، ويتطلب الاستخدام العملي حشوًا مثل OAEP للتشفير وPSS للتوقيعات (Katz وLindell، مقدمة في التشفير الحديث).

transcript.en: A student project stored passwords as plain SHA two fifty six hashes. When the table leaked in a class exercise, a laptop recovered half of them in an afternoon. Today: what a cryptographic hash guarantees, why passwords need salted slow hashes, and where a second factor really helps. A cryptographic hash maps any input to a short fixed-length digest. It should be infeasible to find an input from a digest, or two inputs with the same digest. Change one bit, and the digest changes completely. General hashes are designed to be fast. A graphics card can try billions of guesses a second. People choose predictable passwords, so an attacker hashes a dictionary and looks for matches. Here is the relative rate of guesses on one graphics card. A plain fast hash allows vastly more guesses than a slow, memory-hard function tuned to take a tenth of a second per login. Store passwords with a unique random salt per user and a slow function such as bcrypt, scrypt or Argon two. The salt stops precomputed tables and makes identical passwords look different. The cost factor slows every guess. A second factor means a stolen password alone is not enough. One-time codes help against reuse, but can still be phished. Hardware keys bound to the site's address resist phishing, because they will not sign for a fake domain. Quick check! Two users have the same password. With a unique salt each, what do their stored hashes look like? Different. So an attacker cannot spot shared passwords, and must attack each one separately. A precomputed table for one salt is useless for the next. In the app, open the hash lab. Change one letter of the input and compare the digests, then add a salt and watch identical passwords diverge. Your turn. A staff member typed a password and a one-time code into a fake login page. Which second factor would have stopped the attacker? A hardware security key bound to the real site. Remember: fast hashes are wrong for passwords, salt every user, tune a slow function, and prefer phishing-resistant factors. Try it in your next lab: give teams a small table of fake users hashed three ways. They time a dictionary attack on each, then explain the difference in their report.

title.en: Salts, slow hashes and second factors

body.en:
A cryptographic hash function maps arbitrary input to a fixed-length digest and should resist preimage, second-preimage and collision attacks; a one-bit input change should alter about half the output bits. General-purpose hashes such as SHA-256 are designed to be fast, which is exactly wrong for passwords: a GPU can test billions of candidate passwords per second against a leaked table, and human-chosen passwords are concentrated in a small, guessable space.

Password storage therefore uses a unique random salt per account and a deliberately slow function, preferably a memory-hard one such as Argon2id or scrypt (bcrypt is slow but not memory-hard), with the cost tuned so each verification takes on the order of 100 ms on the server. Salts defeat precomputed tables and hide shared passwords; cost factors multiply the attacker’s work for every guess. Current guidance (NIST SP 800-63B-4, 2025) also favours length over composition rules and checks against breached-password lists.

A second factor means a stolen password alone is insufficient. SMS and app codes resist credential reuse but can be relayed by real-time phishing proxies; FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware keys bind each signature to the site’s origin and so resist phishing. A lab in which students crack a weakly hashed table of synthetic accounts, then repeat against Argon2id, makes the cost difference unforgettable.
body.ar:
تحوّل دالة التجزئة التشفيرية أيَّ مدخل إلى ملخص ثابت الطول، وينبغي أن تقاوم هجمات الصورة الأصلية والصورة الأصلية الثانية والتصادم، وأن يغيّر تغيير بت واحد في المدخل نحو نصف بتات الخرج. والتجزئات العامة مثل SHA-256 مصممة لتكون سريعة، وهذا خطأ تمامًا لكلمات السر: فمعالج الرسوميات يستطيع اختبار مليارات كلمات السر المرشحة في الثانية مقابل جدول مسرّب، وكلمات السر التي يختارها البشر مركّزة في فضاء صغير قابل للتخمين.

لذلك يستخدم تخزين كلمات السر ملحًا عشوائيًا فريدًا لكل حساب ودالة بطيئة عمدًا، ويفضَّل أن تكون كثيفة الذاكرة مثل Argon2id أو scrypt (أما bcrypt فبطيئة لكنها ليست كثيفة الذاكرة)، مع ضبط التكلفة بحيث يستغرق كل تحقق نحو ١٠٠ مللي ثانية على الخادم. والملح يُبطل الجداول المحسوبة مسبقًا ويخفي كلمات السر المشتركة، ومعاملات التكلفة تضاعف جهد المهاجم في كل تخمين. وتفضّل الإرشادات الحالية (NIST SP 800-63B-4 الصادرة عام ٢٠٢٥) أيضًا الطول على قواعد التركيب، وتوصي بالفحص مقابل قوائم كلمات السر المسرّبة.

ويعني العامل الثاني أن كلمة السر المسروقة وحدها لا تكفي. وتقاوم رموز الرسائل النصية والتطبيقات إعادة استخدام بيانات الدخول، لكن وكلاء التصيّد الفوري يستطيعون نقلها، أما مفاتيح الأجهزة بمعيار ⁦FIDO2/WebAuthn⁩ فتربط كل توقيع بمصدر الموقع فتقاوم التصيّد. والمعمل الذي يكسر فيه الطلاب جدولًا مجزّأً تجزئة ضعيفة لحسابات اصطناعية، ثم يكرّرون ذلك مع Argon2id، يجعل فرق التكلفة لا يُنسى.

transcript.en: A keen student practised a network scan from the course on the university's live network. Within minutes, the security team had disabled his account and called our department. Today: the ethics of teaching offensive skills, how to build an isolated lab, and how to assess students with capture-the-flag tasks and write-ups. The same scan is a lesson in a lab and an offence on someone else's network. Many countries criminalise unauthorised access. So teaching offensive skills requires written authorisation, a defined scope, and an isolated environment. Before the first offensive lab, students sign a short code of conduct. It names the lab networks they may test, forbids everything else, explains responsible disclosure, and states the consequences of breaking it. A safe lab can run on one server: virtual machines on a host-only network, no route to the internet or the campus, and snapshots so any machine can be reset in seconds. In a capture-the-flag task, each challenge hides a secret string. Finding it proves the technique worked. Flags are easy to auto-grade, but they can be shared, so the write-up carries most of the marks. Every attack lab should end with defence. After exploiting a flaw, students write the fix, a detection rule, and a short note for a manager. That pairing builds professionals, not just attackers. Quick check! The student scanned the live network. What should the course have provided to prevent this? A signed scope that named the only allowed targets, and an isolated lab where practising was safe. The student needed a place to practise and clear limits. In the app, open the phishing lab. Inspect each message for the signs of a phish, then discuss how you would run a phishing exercise ethically, with consent and no shaming. Your turn. Flags from your last exercise appeared on a public forum. What change to the assessment protects its validity? Per-student flags and graded write-ups. Remember: authorise and scope every offensive task, isolate the lab, and pair every attack with defence. Try it this term: write a one-page code of conduct for your offensive labs. body.en:
Defenders must understand attacks, so university security courses teach offensive techniques. That creates duties for the lecturer: students must know the law (unauthorised access offences exist in most jurisdictions, including computer-misuse and cybercrime laws in Egypt and elsewhere), the professional codes that apply (the ACM Code of Ethics), and the difference between authorised testing and intrusion. A written rules-of-engagement document that states the permitted targets, tools, times and reporting duties, signed by each student, turns a vague norm into an explicit contract.

Practice must happen where mistakes are harmless. Isolated cyber ranges, using virtual machines on a host-only network with no route to campus or the internet, intentionally vulnerable targets, and snapshots for reset, let students attack freely. Responsible-disclosure exercises teach what to do when they find a real flaw.

Capture-the-flag (CTF) exercises motivate and scale, but flags alone measure finding answers, not understanding, and are easily shared. Stronger assessment uses per-student generated flags, graded write-ups that explain the method and the fix, oral spot-checks, and a rubric that rewards defensive reasoning. CTF platforms such as CTFd and the curriculum guidance in ACM/IEEE CSEC2017 support this design.

يجب أن يفهم المدافعون الهجمات، لذا تدرّس مقررات الأمن الجامعية تقنيات هجومية. وهذا يفرض واجبات على المحاضر: يجب أن يعرف الطلاب القانون (فجرائم الوصول غير المصرّح به موجودة في معظم الأنظمة القانونية، ومنها قوانين مكافحة جرائم تقنية المعلومات في مصر وغيرها)، والمواثيق المهنية المنطبقة (ميثاق أخلاقيات ACM)، والفرق بين الاختبار المصرّح به والاختراق. ووثيقة قواعد اشتباك مكتوبة تحدد الأهداف والأدوات والأوقات المسموح بها وواجبات الإبلاغ، يوقّعها كل طالب، تحوّل العُرف الغامض إلى عقد صريح.

ويجب أن يجري التمرين حيث تكون الأخطاء بلا ضرر. فميادين التدريب السيبراني المعزولة، التي تستخدم أجهزة افتراضية على شبكة داخلية لا مسار لها إلى الجامعة أو الإنترنت، مع أهداف ضعيفة عمدًا ولقطات للاستعادة، تتيح للطلاب الهجوم بحرية. وتعلّم تمارين الإفصاح المسؤول ما يجب فعله عند اكتشاف ثغرة حقيقية.

وتحفّز تمارين التقاط العلم (CTF) وتتوسع بسهولة، لكن الأعلام وحدها تقيس إيجاد الإجابات لا الفهم، ويسهل تداولها. والتقييم الأقوى يستخدم أعلامًا مولّدة لكل طالب، وتقارير مقيَّمة تشرح الطريقة والإصلاح، وفحوصًا شفهية مفاجئة، ومعيار تقييم يكافئ التفكير الدفاعي. وتدعم هذا التصميم منصات مثل CTFd وإرشادات المناهج في ⁦ACM/IEEE CSEC2017⁩.
